<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Marine and coastal restoration is essential to achieving global biodiversity and climate targets, yet progress remains slow. One overlooked barrier is that regulatory permitting frameworks for restoration often assess only the risks of undertaking restoration, without considering the risks of inaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aimed to explore whether and how restoration decision‐making should incorporate counterfactual reasoning by explicitly comparing the consequences of action and inaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use a series of global examples to demonstrate how current processes focus on the risks of action, and what the implications of this can be.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identify how existing legal and governance arrangements can reinforce a bias toward the status quo and propose practical reforms, including explicit assessment of the risks of inaction and improved coordination across agencies to support more balanced and evidence‐based restoration decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Legal and governance frameworks requiring consideration of the risks of action and inaction associated with restoration can provide a more accurate picture of the true risks associated with restoration projects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Including the action of inaction in restoration decision‐making: a coastal perspective

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hydrologic extremes such as drought are projected to intensify with climate change, challenging wetland revegetation. Seed‐based restoration is widely used because it is cost‐effective and scalable, but establishment often fails under unsuitable moisture conditions. Two frameworks may improve outcomes under uncertainty: precision restoration, which matches treatments to site conditions, and bet‐hedging, which diversifies strategies to spread risk. These approaches remain largely untested in wetlands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the effects of precision and bet‐hedging seeding strategies on plant community recovery in wetland restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated one precision treatment (5‐species mix) and three bet‐hedging treatments: a diverse species mix, delayed germination, and multi‐year sowing at two hydrologically distinct sites in Great Salt Lake wetlands, Utah, United States. We measured native and invasive plant cover, community composition, and labor and seed costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hydrology dominated restoration outcomes. At Farmington Bay, rapid drying suppressed establishment across all treatments, indicating that neither strategy can overcome severe moisture limitation. At Howard Slough, where soils remained saturated, the precision treatment produced the highest seeded cover in year one. By year 2, seeded cover converged across treatments, but multi‐year sowing reduced invasive cover relative to the unseeded control. Precision and diverse mix treatments required the least labor, whereas multi‐year sowing required approximately 3× more effort but provided the strongest ecological benefits over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Water availability strongly constrains seed‐based wetland revegetation. Precision approaches promote rapid establishment under favorable conditions, whereas repeated sowing can improve longer‐term outcomes by reducing invasive cover, albeit with greater labor demands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Water availability mediates the effectiveness of precision and bet‐hedging seeding strategies in wetland restoration

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drylands experience disturbances that can lead to shifts in plant and microbial communities. Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi help mediate establishment, survival, and resource flow within above‐ and belowground communities and have the potential to be used as a restoration tool to facilitate revegetation under disturbance regimes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To better understand how AM fungal abundance changes with disturbance and examine its restoration potential, we sampled soils across a gradient of sites in the southwestern United States. We hypothesized that (1) AM fungal abundance would be greater in “Reference” compared to “Disturbed” areas, and (2) plant functional group cover at the sampling source would help predict AM fungal abundance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      At six sites, we sampled soil and measured plant functional group cover from paired areas that had documented disturbance with low native plant cover (“Disturbed”) and no or low disturbance with high native plant cover (“Reference”). We compared the mycorrhizal inoculum potential (MIP), a measure of the density of viable propagules of AM fungi, in these soils using two greenhouse bioassays: one with 120
                      <jats:italic>Bouteloua gracilis</jats:italic>
                      plants and the other with 120
                      <jats:italic>Zea mays</jats:italic>
                      plants.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      MIP was greater in Reference than Disturbed areas at five of the six sites in the
                      <jats:italic>B. gracilis</jats:italic>
                      bioassay. Native grass cover was strongly positively correlated with MIP.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results suggest that both disturbance and plant functional group can help predict MIP, and that the presence of native grass seems to consistently correlate with MIP across a range of dryland contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Native grass cover as a field indicator of mycorrhizal inoculum potential in southwestern drylands

<jats:p>
                    Forest restoration projects affect the entire ecosystem; therefore, they require comprehensive environmental monitoring to ensure their success and counteract unexpected challenges. In this context, complementary monitoring indicators should be selected based on available budget and time, along with advanced analytical techniques to enable a cost‐effective, more comprehensive evaluation of ecosystem outcomes. Here, we describe how measuring tree community composition, aboveground biomass of trees, soil nutrients, and soil microbes using high‐throughput sequencing can provide a broader understanding of the restoration trajectory, especially when environmental variables are considered together using machine learning algorithms. As a successful example of this approach, we report the results of a case study conducted in naturally regenerating
                    <jats:italic>Acacia mangium</jats:italic>
                    plantations. Ultimately, this research serves as a robust baseline and validation of the efficiency of advanced techniques for studying complementary indicators of forest restoration across forest biomes and geographic regions.
                  </jats:p>
title: Cost‐effective assessment of forest restoration projects: merging advanced techniques with comprehensive analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High seedling mortality during the establishment phase remains a major constraint for forest restoration in Mediterranean‐type ecosystems, where increasing drought frequency and intensity limit post‐planting performance. Seedling survival under these conditions depends not only on site characteristics and species selection but also on functional traits acquired during nursery cultivation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We evaluated whether reducing nursery fertilization induces functional traits and physiological responses associated with drought tolerance, and whether these responses improve field survival of
                      <jats:italic>Cryptocarya alba</jats:italic>
                      , a native Mediterranean tree species widely used in restoration programs in central Chile.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seedlings were grown under contrasting fertilization regimes, exposed to a controlled drought experiment, and subsequently outplanted across contrasting slope aspects representing different levels of water limitation. Morphological traits, physiological responses, and post‐planting survival were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Reduced fertilization altered seedling morphology and biomass allocation and, particularly under low nitrogen (low N) availability, allowed seedlings to maintain photosynthetic activity under drought. However, these responses did not translate into improved field survival. Control seedlings showed higher final survival than seedlings grown under low N and low nitrogen–phosphorus fertilization, whereas the low phosphorus treatment did not differ significantly from the control. Survival also differed between slope aspects and among restoration sites, but the fertilization × slope interaction was not significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Physiological responses to drought induced during nursery cultivation were insufficient to improve field establishment when accompanied by substantial reductions in seedling growth. For
                      <jats:italic>C. alba</jats:italic>
                      , reduced nursery fertilization therefore provided no advantage for post‐planting survival under the conditions evaluated.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Nursery fertilization shapes physiological drought responses but does not enhance field survival in Cryptocarya alba from Mediterranean central Chile

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoration of afforested peatlands aims to recover biodiversity, but evidence for long‐term bird responses remains limited. In Scotland's Flow Country, conifer plantations established during the 1970s and 1980s displaced breeding waders and created edge effects on adjacent bog. Forest‐to‐bog restoration began in the 1990s and expanded during the 2000s.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To assess whether relationships between breeding wader occupancy and historical forest edges differ between standing plantations and areas where forest has been removed for restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We surveyed 171 km
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      of open peatland during 2022–2024, approximately two decades after an earlier survey. We recorded 1951 species‐by‐square occurrences of Dunlin (
                      <jats:italic>Calidris alpina</jats:italic>
                      ), Golden plover (
                      <jats:italic>Pluvialis apricaria</jats:italic>
                      ), and Greenshank (
                      <jats:italic>Tringa nebularia</jats:italic>
                      ). Presence–absence models assessed associations with forest proximity, environmental characteristics, and historical forest edge status.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Golden plover showed a weaker occupancy relationship with distance from restoration edges than standing‐forest edges. Dunlin showed a similar pattern, although evidence for differing distance relationships was weaker. Forest proximity remained associated with occupancy for both species. Greenshank showed limited evidence of a strong overall forest edge effect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Contemporary occupancy patterns are consistent with reduced historical forest edge effects following plantation removal, particularly for Golden plover. However, these observational comparisons cannot establish causal effects or directly quantify temporal occupancy change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Responses of peatland waders to large‐scale, non‐native forestry removal: measuring changes in edge effects after 20 years

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Habitat loss and degradation threaten many taxa, and restoring habitats requires understanding how management influences resource availability for imperiled species. Restoration often focuses on plant composition, yet identifying plants that support essential trophic interactions remains a critical need. Maritime grasslands are an imperiled, understudied ecosystem where this knowledge is limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We quantified trophic interactions at a maritime grassland restoration reference site to identify plants providing key resources for a declining omnivorous songbird, the Painted Bunting (
                      <jats:italic>Passerina ciris</jats:italic>
                      ).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using fecal DNA metabarcoding and field‐based food availability sampling, we quantified plant and insect taxa in Painted Bunting diets, evaluated seasonal diet variation relative to resource availability, and developed a restoration importance index to prioritize plant taxa in restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found that bunting diets changed throughout the breeding season and that birds consumed food resources proportional to resource availability, suggesting that buntings do not show a strong food‐type preference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results demonstrate the value of incorporating trophic interactions from reference sites to guide habitat restoration for species of conservation concern and a transferable framework for restoration efforts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Trophic relationships at a restoration reference site identify key plant resources for a declining songbird

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoring ecological function and stability is crucial amid anthropogenic biodiversity loss. Yet, taxonomic diversity alone provides an incomplete picture, requiring incorporation of functional and phylogenetic diversity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated how boreal deciduous forest restoration influences functional and phylogenetic diversity of saproxylic beetle communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We compared non‐restored forests, forests restored 12–21 years earlier by removing conifers to benefit deciduous trees, and restoration target forests. Restoration targeted the deciduous umbrella species, the White‐backed woodpecker (
                      <jats:italic>Dendrocopos leucotos</jats:italic>
                      ).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restored forests supported less phylogenetic richness than target forests. Their functional composition was closer to that of non‐restored forests while phylogenetic composition differed among all forest types. These differences were associated with lower relative abundances of large‐bodied and deciduous‐associated species in restored forests compared to target forests. The target forests also had greater functional divergence, indicating that abundance was distributed toward more extreme traits. At landscape scale, we found no differences in phylogenetic or functional richness between forest types, suggesting that restoration altered local diversity, while many species and traits occurred across restored stands collectively. However, target forests supported greater functional diversity when frequent and dominant species were given more weight, showing landscape‐scale differences remained in trait‐abundance distributions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoration altered saproxylic beetle communities but, after 12–21 years, had not recreated the functional and phylogenetic structure of target forests. Restored communities were distinct rather than consistently intermediate between non‐restored and target conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Deciduous forest restoration alters but does not restore functional and phylogenetic diversity of saproxylic beetles

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deforestation and fires have caused substantial loss of tropical peat swamp forests (PSF) in Southeast Asia. Substantial efforts have been undertaken to rewet and revegetate peatlands, but these restoration measures can lead to conflicting outcomes. Knowledge is needed on how to combine revegetation and rewetting approaches to effectively restore peatlands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using a large‐scale field manipulation in Sumatra, Indonesia, on a former
                      <jats:italic>Acacia</jats:italic>
                      plantation on peat, the effects of water table depth (WTD) below the peat surface and shading conditions on planted tree species were tested.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      WTD was manipulated through surface treatments by lowering the peat surface to differing depths (0, −0.25, and −0.50 m) and carried out shading manipulation across 72 plots with a complementary natural
                      <jats:italic>Acacia</jats:italic>
                      tree shading experiment in 12 plots. Individual tree survival and growth of 3124 seedlings from 16 species were monitored from 24 up to 36 months, alongside natural regeneration.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Higher water tables with prolonged inundation inhibited seedling growth, survival, and natural regeneration. Full shade treatment with artificial netting increased seedling survival but reduced growth during the first 12 months. Similar effects were observed in the natural
                      <jats:italic>Acacia</jats:italic>
                      tree shading experiment. There were significant species differences in response to treatments and continuous WTD variation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings showcase that too much rewetting has the potential to negatively influence planted seedling growth and survival and highlight the importance of shading to ensure seedling survival. These insights provide a foundation for defining optimal WTD targets and species selection strategies for PSF restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Large‐scale rewetting and shading experiment reveals optimum conditions for tropical peat swamp forest restoration

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoring dryland ecosystems under ongoing global change is increasingly urgent, yet efforts are constrained by limited ecological and functional knowledge of native species. Particularly, comparative evidence on how successional species respond to herbivory remains scarce, limiting the development of effective restoration strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate dryland successional species response to biomass removal, testing the role of life‐history traits and plant size in post‐disturbance (grazing) recovery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a greenhouse experiment applying clipping treatments to simulate grazing on juvenile plants of four native species (two early‐ and two intermediate‐successional). We quantified mortality and growth responses (height, diameter, volume, and branch and leaf production). Late‐successional species were not included due to limited seedling availability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Growth responses differed significantly among successional types, species identity, and clipping intensity. Smaller, early‐successional species generally showed faster and greater recovery than larger, intermediate species and differed in their allocation to apical versus lateral growth following clipping. Intermediate species displayed contrasting responses, with slight lateral compensation in one species and reduced growth in the other.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recovery from biomass loss was primarily driven by life‐history strategy and life‐form rather than plant size. Early‐successional species displayed rapid, opportunistic responses, whereas intermediate species exhibited more conservative strategies, potentially linked to slower resource reallocation and/or lower tolerance to disturbance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From overgrazing to restoration: recovery strategies of dryland species after biomass removal

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Microbial amendments can improve restorations by increasing plant performance and decreasing soil erosion. Whole‐soil amendments collected from native ecosystems, in particular, can produce desirable outcomes; however, it is unclear if all native soil amendments produce equally positive effects. Instead, it is likely that donor locations differ in their microbial communities, which may change their efficacy for restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We tested whether soil amendments sourced from sites across the Texas Gulf Coast differed in their effects on aboveground and belowground responses, and whether donor site characteristics predicted the efficacy of the soil amendments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a greenhouse experiment, a community of five native plant species was grown in live or sterilized soil amendments collected from 11 sites.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In comparison to sterile amendments, live amendments improved plant biomass, plant diversity, arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungal colonization, and density of AM fungal extra‐radical hyphae (ERH), a metric strongly connected to soil stability. One soil amendment origin outperformed the others, with an almost three‐fold increase in total plant biomass and an almost six‐fold increase in ERH compared to other live treatments. The performance of amendments was positively correlated to plant species richness and ERH at the donor sites.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Where native soil amendments are sourced from could dramatically alter restoration outcomes. While amendments generally outperformed sterile soil, one location clearly outperformed the others by increasing plant biomass and soil stability, suggesting that careful selection of microbial amendments can be useful for optimizing restorations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Variation in the effectiveness of native microbial amendments for coastal dune restoration

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Biodiversity offsetting aims to achieve no net loss of ecosystem functions by compensating unavoidable impacts. Germany has enforced a legally binding impact mitigation regulation (Eingriffsregelung) since 1976 using numerical eco‐point scoring systems, yet its long‐term ecological effectiveness remains poorly understood. We evaluated long‐term restoration outcomes of compensation measures in North Rhine–Westphalia across complementary indicators of target habitat attainment, numerical target‐value achievement, and restoration progress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Combining archival reconstruction with field mapping following official assessment frameworks, we analysed 74 compensation measures (>20 years old, comprising 661 habitat units, 408.9 ha) in the Lower Rhine Lowlands. We assessed target habitat attainment, numerical target‐value achievement, numerical target deviation (ΔTarget), and an adapted Achieved Restoration index AR) using mixed‐effects models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, 64% of habitat units achieved their numerical target score, whereas only 17% attained their intended target habitat type. Forests showed favourable outcomes, while grasslands showed low target attainment and restoration performance. Larger habitat units performed generally better. Although restoration age positively correlated with AR, older sites did not show progressive convergence toward intended target habitat states.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Numerical target‐value achievement occurred far more frequently than target habitat‐type attainment, demonstrating that standardized eco‐point scoring metrics can mask major structural and compositional divergence. Long‐term outcomes were heavily influenced by habitat‐specific successional dynamics, site conditions, and management histories, with grassland habitats particularly prone to target failure due to unmanaged forest succession.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Long‐term restoration outcomes in biodiversity offsetting: evaluating 20 years of habitat development and target attainment

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Quarry restoration in Mediterranean regions such as Cyprus is expected to face more intensive problems than neighboring reference habitats due to effects of their recent disturbance, size, and isolation. Epigeic arthropod biodiversity can provide useful clues on restoration success.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We assessed diversity of restored and reference areas at 10 quarry sites in Cyprus. Ecological and functional diversity (FD) of two epigeic beetle families (Carabidae and Tenebrionidae), directly influenced by landscape changes and disturbance, is used for such an assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Areas were sampled twice via pitfall traps in 2024. Age, connectivity, landscape diversity, patch size, and organic amendment application were examined as potential drivers of diversity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restorations supported reduced diversity and activity‐density, indicating either negative effects of restoration practices on specialist taxa and the promotion of communities with functionally similar species, or the effects of ecological succession leading to relaxation of diversity below expected levels due to isolation and small size of restored areas. Unexpectedly, restoration age negatively affected diversity, corroborating the latter interpretation. Also, restored areas with higher connectivity exhibit increased diversity, while the size of restorations is negatively associated with diversity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>FD approaches can reveal diversity responses not observed by abundance/richness data alone. Functionality in restoration areas can decrease with time as long as these are not fully integrated with surrounding habitats, a finding that can inform management practices so that they can further promote connectivity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Restoration age, landscape diversity, and connectivity affect epigeic beetle diversity in multiple aggregates' quarries of Cyprus

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>River fragmentation disrupts ecological connectivity, constraining the movement, recruitment, and persistence of migratory fishes. Although fishways are widely implemented to mitigate these impacts, most evidence of effectiveness derives from northern hemisphere systems dominated by large‐bodied salmonids. Consequently, uncertainty remains as to whether common fishway designs are effective for small‐bodied, often diadromous fishes characteristic of temperate southern hemisphere rivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated the long‐term, regional‐scale influence of barrier mitigation on the occupancy dynamics of two model fish species in a temperate southern hemisphere river network.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We analyzed a 45‐year composite dataset of presence–absence records from 25 sub‐catchments across five river basins in Greater Melbourne, Australia, where low‐head, lower‐catchment barriers have been progressively mitigated using standard fishway types. Dynamic occupancy models accounting for imperfect detection were used to estimate colonization, extinction, and occupancy trajectories for diadromous Common galaxias (
                      <jats:italic>Galaxias maculatus</jats:italic>
                      ) and potadromous Flathead gudgeon (
                      <jats:italic>Philypnodon grandiceps</jats:italic>
                      ).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Occupancy dynamics of Common galaxias were strongly associated with barrier mitigation. Colonization probability increased threefold following mitigation, producing rapid catchment‐scale expansion over the period of barrier mitigation and persistent occupancy thereafter. In contrast, Flathead gudgeon showed gradual increases in occupancy over time but no strong response to barrier status.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoring longitudinal connectivity enabled rapid recolonization and sustained occupancy for a diadromous fish at a regional scale, providing rare long‐term evidence of fishway effectiveness in a temperate southern hemisphere context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Long‐term restoration of river connectivity drives recovery of a diadromous fish in southern Australia

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The worldwide decline of coral reefs has led to the proliferation of local‐scale coral restoration projects. Active restoration using in‐water coral tree nurseries and outplanting of coral fragments is relatively new on the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) and complements traditional, passive approaches to reef protection. However, given the infancy of these methods, few studies have measured the effectiveness of coral restoration techniques, including coral nursery systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The study aimed to assess the performance of 10
                      <jats:italic>Acropora</jats:italic>
                      species commonly used in coral tree nurseries and evaluate the impacts of harvesting wild colonies for small‐scale coral restoration programs at Hastings Reef and Fitzroy Island in the central GBR.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wild reef colonies were selected as donor colonies and harvested to create fragments for coral tree nurseries. Donor and untouched (control) wild colonies were monitored for 6 months for bleaching, predation, disease, mortality, and growth. Fragment health and growth in a nursery were compared with wild and donor colonies. Species performance within nurseries was also compared. Data were analyzed using generalized linear models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All species showed increased growth rates after 6 months in a nursery, with lower predation and disease than control colonies on a nearby reef. However, nursery corals exhibited higher bleaching, likely due to higher temperatures at the shallower depths where nurseries were located.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Harvesting fragments had no negative effect on donor colony health. Multiple
                      <jats:italic>Acropora</jats:italic>
                      species benefited from the nursery environment and could help maintain local diversity and increase coral abundance. Higher bleaching rates in nursery fragments indicate that thermal stress must be mitigated.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Acropora species on the Great Barrier Reef's first coral tree nursery
